name: SLEEF (SIMD Library for Evaluating Elementary Functions)
baseline: <cmath> (scalar libm, represented in the paper by FDLIBM as the reference scalar implementation)
workload: Reciprocal throughput (ns/call) of sin/cos/tan/log/exp/pow etc. over random arguments across several domains, single-threaded tight loop executed 10^10 times, measured with clock_gettime
claimed_speedup: From Table 2 (reciprocal throughput, ns): sin 1-ulp domain [0,1e+100]: FDLIBM 162.3 vs SLEEF 48.79 (~3.3x); cos same domain: 162.1 vs 50.38 (~3.2x); tan same domain: 177.0 vs 48.82 (~3.6x); log domain [0,1e+300]: 31.66 vs 15.46 (~2.0x); exp domain [-700,700]: 12.19 vs 7.663 (~1.6x); on the narrow domain [0.4,0.5] SLEEF is roughly at parity with FDLIBM (e.g. sin: 11.43 vs 11.41). (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: SLEEF and FDLIBM compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma; Vector-libm compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize -ftree-vectorizer-verbose=1 -fno-math-errno; SVML via Intel C Compiler 19 with -fimf-max-error=1.0/4.0
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 CPU @ 3.40GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (physical PC, no VM)
tradeoffs: Vectorized code takes the slow path for a whole SIMD register if any lane needs it; library offers a 1-ULP and a faster 3.5-ULP accuracy tier as a speed/accuracy tradeoff; on narrow argument domains the scalar-equivalent speed roughly ties FDLIBM rather than beating it, the win is concentrated in wide-domain/branchy cases and true vector (multi-lane) throughput.
caveats: The paper (IEEE TPDS, peer-reviewed, arXiv preprint used here) compares against FDLIBM, a specific reference libm implementation, not directly against libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::sin/std::exp as shipped, though many system libms derive from similar algorithms; the sleef.org benchmark page itself (https://sleef.org/benchmark.xhtml) only compares against Intel SVML, not libm, so that page was not used as the evidence source. Public availability of the exact benchmark harness used for Table 2 was not independently confirmed in this session, so tier is capped at B rather than A.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "vectorized math library faster than std::exp std::sin benchmark C++" led to the SLEEF arXiv paper; repo confirmed via gh api repos/shibatch/sleef

name: VDT (VectoriseD maTh)
workload: Scalar double-precision exp/log/sin/cos/tan/asin/acos/atan/isqrt time in ns/call over an input interval of roughly [-5000,5000] (function-dependent), plus SSE and AVX vectorized variants
hardware: Intel Core i7-3930K CPU @ 3.20GHz, Scientific Linux 6
stars_or_usage: 59 stars; used in LHC experiment software and the Geant4 simulation toolkit at CERN
tradeoffs: Results are approximate (documented average bit-level difference vs libm per function, e.g. up to ~0.45 ULP for isqrt); functions live in a separate vdt:: namespace with fast_ prefixes rather than being a drop-in for std math calls, though a PRELOAD build mode can intercept libm calls at runtime.
caveats: README benchmark table does not state the compiler or optimization flags used to produce the numbers (only CPU/OS), so per the hard rules this is capped at tier C rather than A; hardware is an older (~2012) CPU generation.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "vectorized math library faster than std::exp std::sin benchmark C++" surfaced a Cornell test file referencing VDT (stressVdt.cxx); repo located via gh search repos "vdt vectorised math" and confirmed with gh api repos/dpiparo/vdt

name: LibRapid
workload: Elementwise matrix expression res = aa * bb - cc on 1000x1000 double matrices, run repeatedly (~15,000 iterations) and timed
claimed_speedup: 558.71% faster (~5.6x): LibRapid Array 284.405us vs nested std::vector<std::vector<double>> loops 1.589ms
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.33, default project settings; LibRapid 'Optimise Small Arrays' option OFF
tradeoffs: Baseline used is naive nested std::vector<std::vector<double>> loops rather than std::valarray or a vectorization-friendly std::transform/std::reduce pipeline, so the comparison is somewhat favorable to LibRapid; large template-based array/tensor library with its own memory layout and (optional) Python bindings, so adoption is a bigger commitment than a header drop-in.
caveats: First-party blog-post benchmark from the project's own account; single workload, single hardware/compiler configuration, and only 'default settings' given for MSVC flags (not fully enumerated); baseline is std::vector rather than the specific std::valarray/std::transform/std::reduce facilities named for this category, hence baseline_in_list=false.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "'std::valarray' benchmark 'times faster' SIMD library github" surfaced a dev.to LibRapid post; repo confirmed via gh search repos "librapid" and gh api repos/LibRapid/librapid

name: fmath (herumi)
workload: Array-mode natural log and exponential over float arrays (fmath_logf_v / fmath_expf_v), average CPU cycles per 32 elements, using AVX2/AVX-512
claimed_speedup: Linux Xeon w9-3495X (AVX-512): logf_v 15.7x, expf_v 18.5x faster than std. Windows Core i7-1165G7 (AVX-512): logf_v 16.9x, expf_v 19.5x. Windows Core i7-1255U (no AVX-512): logf_v 9.4x, expf_v 12.9x.
hardware: Xeon w9-3495X (Linux, AVX-512); Core i7-1165G7 (Windows, AVX-512); Core i7-1255U (Windows, no AVX-512)
tradeoffs: Array-only API operating on raw float buffers (not a drop-in replacement for scalar std::logf/std::expf calls); requires AVX2 as a minimum, auto-upgrades to AVX-512; author explicitly warns against use for small n (<16) because it is slower than std there; single precision only.
caveats: GitHub's automatic license detector reports no LICENSE file for this repo (license: null in repo metadata); the BSD-3-Clause claim comes from text in readme.md itself, not a separate LICENSE file, so this should be double-checked before treating the code as unambiguously licensed. Benchmark table states CPU model and OS but not compiler or optimization flags.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fmath fast exp SIMD" -> gh api repos/herumi/fmath, confirmed via repos/herumi/fmath/contents/readme.md

name: FastMath C++ Library (fast_math_cpp)
baseline: <cmath> (std::sinh, std::tanh, std::atanh, std::atan2, std::pow, std::acos, std::log10, std::tan, std::exp, std::log, etc.)
workload: 1,000,000 scalar calls per function across 28 function/domain combinations (trig, hyperbolic, exp/log family, rounding), best-of-25 interleaved runs, benchmarked on x86_64 (GCC 11.4) and Raspberry Pi 4 (GCC 12.2); also a batch/array SIMD API for sin/cos/sincos/atan2
claimed_speedup: Scalar calls, x86_64 -> Raspberry Pi 4: sinh 2.96x->3.94x, tanh 2.94x->3.91x, atanh 2.42x->2.49x, atan2 2.18x/1.63x, integer pow (base^2) 2.02x->4.54x, acos 1.76x/1.57x, log10 1.45x->2.20x, tan 1.44x/1.40x; batch/array API for sin/cos/sincos/atan2 is 2-6x over scalar loops. Author also reports 21 of 28 scalar functions match-or-beat std on both platforms, and explicitly documents cases where it is at parity or slower: exp/log/log2/sqrt sit at 0.94x-1.01x, and scalar sin/cos/sincos needing range reduction run at 0.63x-0.88x on ARM.
compiler_and_flags: Both library and baseline built with identical flags via the fast_math_bench target: -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops
hardware: x86_64: Linux 6.6, GCC 11.4 (exact CPU model not stated); Raspberry Pi 4 (BCM2711 SoC): Linux 6.12 aarch64, GCC 12.2
tradeoffs: Header-only; several functions (exp, log, log2, sqrt) are deliberately thin wrappers over std:: because the author's own polynomial attempts could not beat glibc's table-based implementations; scalar sin/cos/sincos regress vs std on ARM for angles needing range reduction; author documents 5-10% run-to-run variance and treats anything under 1.1x as a tie.
caveats: Very small, low-visibility personal project (2 stars, likely a solo hobby/robotics-adjacent effort). Exact x86 CPU model is not given (only 'x86_64, Linux 6.6'), so despite public benchmark code and stated compiler flags this falls short of tier A's CPU-model requirement and is capped at C. The README is unusually transparent about negative/parity results, which increases confidence in the reported positive numbers even though the project is obscure.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "'Faster Math Functions, Soundly' github repository code libm benchmark" surfaced hijimasa/fast_math_cpp; confirmed via gh api repos/hijimasa/fast_math_cpp and its README.md
